title: Observability export protocol consolidation and OpenTelemetry bench + serializer refactor
creator: Maya Patel
description:
Problem: Over time we've accumulated several competing telemetry exporters and a custom binary envelope used by internal sinks. This has increased runtime binary size, raised steady-state memory allocations (high-allocation paths during high QPS), and added maintenance overhead because each exporter pulls in heavyweight serialization dependencies.

Goal: Consolidate export protocols where feasible, upgrade the OpenTelemetry SDK to a stable supported release, and replace the heavy custom serializer with a streaming protobuf/OTLP path. The work should reduce allocations and flush latency, shrink observability-related dependency surface area, and provide a benchmark harness that can be used to gate future changes.

Scope:
- Upgrade OpenTelemetry SDK to v1.20.x across runtime and telemetry service.
- Introduce an OTLP/gRPC primary exporter with a light-weight fallback for overloaded private deployments.
- Replace custom capnp-like envelope serializer with a streaming OTLP protobuf marshaller that uses preallocated buffers/zero-copy where possible.
- Remove the legacy "telemetry-serializer-heavy" dependency from runtime builds and move any required bits to an opt-in plugin in telemetry repo.
- Add microbench and end-to-end throughput/latency tests (bench harness) for traces, metrics, and logs under realistic token lengths and batching distributions.
- Define a rollout plan with canaries and automatic rollback triggers tied to memory/latency regressions.

Why this matters: Observability cost is visible in both performance and operational burden. Improving telemetry sigma reduces tail latency risk and speeds up future observability feature development (e.g., per-tenant aggregation).
acceptance_criteria:
1) OpenTelemetry SDK upgrade completes with no semver-breaking runtime regressions and unit test coverage for new instrumentation adapters.
2) Default runtime uses OTLP/gRPC exporter; legacy envelope path is behind a feature flag and removable in a follow-up.
3) Memory allocations in the hot path (trace creation + export) measured with the bench harness show >=30% reduction in p95 allocations compared to baseline.
4) Export flush p99 under simulated steady 5k rps workload is <50ms and CPU usage reduced by >=15% in benchmarked configs.
5) PRs merged include a bench harness and CI perf job that fails on regressions greater than 10% for p95 allocs or p99 latency.
6) Rollout doc and rollback playbook published in Confluence and linked from PR.
notes: Spike findings (2026-02-28): the custom envelope allocates per-span buffers and copies logs twice during batching; switching to streaming OTLP eliminates one copy and allows reuse of buffers between flushes.
Decision (2026-03-03): upgrade OTEL to 1.20.x; keep the legacy sink behind a feature flag for two weeks of canary traffic before removal.
Trade-off: protobuf marshalling complexity increases code surface but yields measurable allocation and latency wins; we will encapsulate marshalling in a small internal package with clear tests.
PR feedback (2026-03-08): security requested an additional KMS-to-exporter handshake review for private deployments; added to security review list.
Bench results (canary subset, 2026-03-09): p95 allocs down 36%, p99 export latency down from 210ms to 42ms (after streaming marshaller). CPU median improved ~18% on c5d-equivalent nodes.
